GaiaFlow: Semantic-Guided Diffusion Tuning for Carbon-Frugal Search

Rong Fu ††thanks: Corresponding author: mc46603@um.edu.mo Affiliation: University of Macau Email: mc46603@um.edu.mo    Wenxin Zhang Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Email: zwxzhang12@163.com    Jia Yee Tan Affiliation: Renmin University of China Email: tanjiayi2002@ruc.edu.cn    Chunlei Meng Affiliation: Fudan University Email: clmeng23@m.fudan.edu.cn    Shuo Yin Affiliation: Tsinghua University Email: yins25@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn    Xiaowen Ma Affiliation: Zhejiang University Email: xwma@zju.edu.cn    Wangyu Wu Affiliation: University of Liverpool Email: v11dryad@foxmail.com    Muge Qi Affiliation: Peking University Email: 2301210659@stu.pku.edu.cn    Guangzhen Yao Affiliation: Northeast Normal University Email: yaoguangzhen@nenu.edu.cn    Zhaolu Kang Affiliation: Peking University Email: kangzl9966@gmail.com    Zeli Su Affiliation: Minzu University of China Email: rickamorty@muc.edu.cn    Simon Fong Affiliation: University of Macau Email: ccfong@um.edu.mo
Abstract

As the burgeoning power requirements of sophisticated neural architectures escalate, the information retrieval community has recognized ecological sustainability as a pivotal priority that necessitates a fundamental paradigm shift in model design. While contemporary neural rankers have attained unprecedented accuracy, the substantial environmental externalities associated with their computational intensity often remain overlooked in large-scale deployments. We present GaiaFlow, an innovative framework engineered to facilitate carbon-frugal search by operationalizing semantic-guided diffusion tuning. Our methodology orchestrates the convergence of retrieval-guided Langevin dynamics and a hardware-independent performance modeling strategy to optimize the trade-off between search precision and environmental preservation. By incorporating adaptive early exit protocols and precision-aware quantized inference, the proposed architecture significantly mitigates operational carbon footprints while maintaining robust retrieval quality across heterogeneous computing infrastructures. Extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate that GaiaFlow achieves a superior equilibrium between effectiveness and energy efficiency, offering a scalable and sustainable pathway for next-generation neural search systems.

   

Keywords Carbon-Frugal Search, Diffusion Tuning, Performance Modeling, Sustainable Information Retrieval

1 Introduction

The ecological footprint of neural information retrieval (IR) architectures has become a central concern as the energy requirements of global data centers continue to escalate [1]. While contemporary neural search paradigms have achieved unprecedented levels of effectiveness, their operational deployment involves significant carbon emissions and substantial water consumption [2, 3]. Recent academic discourse has emphasized the necessity for rigorous carbon footprint accounting within large language models and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frameworks to mitigate these environmental externalities [3, 4, 5, 6]. Historically, however, the assessment of IR efficiency has remained narrowly focused on quantifying query latency, largely due to established evidence that sluggish search performance negatively impacts user satisfaction [7, 8].

Quantifying search efficiency presents unique challenges that are distinct from measuring effectiveness, primarily because of the vast heterogeneity in model architectures, software dependencies, and hardware environments [7, 9]. Existing benchmarking platforms often demand prohibitive computational resources for exhaustive evaluation, which paradoxically increases the environmental cost of the research process itself [7]. Furthermore, a significant portion of current literature prioritizes accuracy gains without adequately addressing the trade-offs between system throughput and environmental frugality [10, 11]. Although innovations such as semantic-enhanced indexing and pseudo-relevance feedback have improved retrieval depth, they frequently introduce structural complexities that complicate energy-efficient execution [12, 13].

To resolve these systemic contradictions, we introduce GaiaFlow, a novel framework that leverages semantic-guided diffusion tuning to facilitate carbon-aware retrieval. Our methodology draws inspiration from recent breakthroughs in diffusion models and Langevin dynamics, which allow for structured navigation within latent manifold geometries [14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. By reconfiguring retrieval-guided Langevin dynamics, GaiaFlow optimizes the search trajectory to eliminate redundant computational operations. We adopt a hardware-agnostic efficiency metric based on cumulative memory and floating-point operation counts, circumventing the volatility of environment-dependent latency measurements [7]. Additionally, the framework incorporates exponentially weighted moving models and early exit strategies to dynamically recalibrate the computational budget according to the complexity of the input query [19, 11].

Our contributions are as follows. First, we present GaiaFlow, a unified and theoretically grounded framework for carbon-conscious neural retrieval that applies semantic-guided diffusion tuning to jointly improve retrieval accuracy and environmental sustainability. This architecture integrates generative diffusion processes with ranking objectives, enabling efficient adaptation of retrieval models while reducing unnecessary computational expenditure. Second, we design a retrieval-guided Langevin sampler that enhances the efficiency of navigating high-dimensional embedding manifolds, allowing the model to reach high-quality representations with fewer inference steps and substantially lowering energy consumption during retrieval. Third, we introduce a hardware-independent performance modeling methodology based on operational counts that provides standardized and reproducible estimates of carbon footprint across heterogeneous system configurations, capturing the intrinsic computational work of retrieval algorithms through memory and floating-point operation analysis. Finally, we offer extensive empirical evidence demonstrating that GaiaFlow achieves a superior effectiveness-to-energy balance compared to existing neural retrieval systems, maintains robustness across diverse hardware platforms, and contributes practical tools and datasets that support future advancements in sustainable information retrieval.

2 Related Work

2.1 Sustainability and Carbon-Aware Computing Systems

Growing concern over the environmental impact of large-scale computing has driven research on carbon-aware system design and management. Foundational work quantified data center carbon footprints by analyzing traffic behavior, Power Usage Effectiveness, and their implications for emission reduction [20, 21]. Recent progress emphasizes real-time operational strategies, including adaptive capacity provisioning enabled by digital twins and workload sharing combined with carbon allowance trading [22, 23]. Advances in hardware and software co-design improve lifecycle assessments by incorporating embodied carbon accounting through retrieval-augmented methods [24, 3]. System-level mechanisms such as carbon-aware operating-system daemons and quality adaptation for energy-intensive services further reinforce sustainability objectives [25, 26]. At the organizational level, large language models now support corporate carbon analysis and climate knowledge systems, enabling more interactive and data-driven decision-making [6].

2.2 Evolution of Semantic Information Retrieval

Modern information retrieval has evolved from lexical matching to deep semantic modeling, with dense passage retrieval enabling effective open-domain question answering through shared embedding spaces [27]. Efficiency-oriented advances include sparse neural retrieval and unified sparse representation frameworks that jointly optimize indexing and retrieval [28, 29]. Search precision is further improved by enhanced swarm algorithms and semantic similarity modeling [30]. Domain-adaptive retrieval benefits from dynamic confidence sampling, label semantic guidance, and semantic-guided hashing for cross-domain alignment [31, 32]. Architectural innovations such as in-storage processing and differentiable search indices strengthen scalability and retrieval speed [33, 34]. Large language model–based query expansion and predictive performance analytics also contribute to better modeling of complex user intent [35, 36].

2.3 Generative Diffusion Models for Optimization and Retrieval

Diffusion-based generative models have advanced high-resolution synthesis and combinatorial optimization, demonstrating strong capability in structured generation tasks [37, 38, 39]. They are increasingly applied to temporal reasoning and score-based modeling through time-series forecasting and stochastic differential equation formulations [40, 41]. For retrieval, diffusion-augmented methods support interactive text-to-image search and controllable music generation, achieving finer multimodal alignment [42, 43]. Diffusion models also act as constrained samplers that explore unknown optimization constraints, while alternating phase Langevin sampling strengthens priors for signal recovery [44, 14]. Passive Langevin dynamics further provide finite-sample guarantees for adaptive inverse reinforcement learning [45]. Chain-of-thought enhancements within diffusion retrieval systems improve sponsored search and recommendation by introducing structured reasoning pathways [46, 47].

2.4 Architectural Efficiency and Resource-Constrained Inference

Research on resource-efficient search and retrieval emphasizes lightweight architectures and energy-aware inference to reduce computational overhead [48]. Differentiable neural architecture search identifies hardware-adaptive designs suitable for constrained embedded platforms and supports sustainable edge intelligence [49, 50]. Inference latency is reduced through early exit mechanisms and retrieval-augmented approaches that skip unnecessary computation during execution [11, 51]. Latency-aware query and prediction systems further simplify multi-platform deployment by maintaining dynamic performance databases [52]. Probabilistic learning methods such as stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics and Gumbel-Softmax reparameterization offer scalable solutions for training complex models [53, 54]. Carbon-aware partitioning of deep neural networks and contrastive visual representation learning ensure that strong model performance remains compatible with strict energy constraints [55, 56].

3 Methodology

This section formalizes our approach to performance modeling and to configuration optimization guided by query semantics. We first describe a differentiable extension of the PEIR symbolic work model that yields smooth carbon and latency surrogates. Next we introduce a latent parameterization with a diffusion prior, a query–configuration retrieval model trained by contrastive learning, and a retrieval-guided Langevin sampler that combines energy descent with semantic attraction. Finally, we present an online calibration loop that updates the latency and carbon mappings from measured data.

3.1 Problem definition

We consider per-query configuration selection as a constrained optimization executed at retrieval time. Let qq denote an incoming query, let ω\omega be a concrete configuration in the feasible set 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and let DD be the decoder mapping latent vectors zz to soft configurations ω^\hat{\omega}. The goal is to select a configuration that minimizes a weighted combination of carbon and latency while satisfying a minimum retrieval-quality requirement. The formulation in latent space reads

z⋆=arg⁡minz∈𝒵⁡U⁡(D⁡(z))subject toQ⁡(D⁡(z),q)≥ρq,z^{\star}\;=\;\arg\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\;U\bigl(D(z)\bigr)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Q\bigl(D(z),q\bigr)\;\geq\;\rho_{q}, (1)

where U⁡(⋅)U(\cdot) is the differentiable green potential combining carbon, latency and effectiveness; Q⁡(⋅,q)Q(\cdot,q) is a fast quality estimator (for example recall or the distilled effectiveness score) evaluated for query qq; ρq\rho_{q} is a query-dependent quality threshold; and 𝒵\mathcal{Z} denotes the learned latent manifold. Here the decoder DD and the quality surrogate QQ are used to ensure constraints are checked rapidly during sampling.

3.2 GaiaFlow algorithm

The compact pseudocode is presented in Algorithm 1. GaiaFlow implements the optimization in Equation (1) by sampling on a latent manifold and biasing trajectories with a retrieval-derived attraction term; this produces candidate configurations that are simultaneously energy-frugal and semantically suitable for the query. The algorithm is designed for low latency through a combination of cache fast-paths, early-exit, quantized evaluation, and guarded online calibration.

3.3 Differentiable PEIR with monotonicity guarantees

PEIR (Performance Estimation for Information Retrieval) is a hardware-agnostic framework that predicts query latency by counting memory and floating-point operations instead of measuring wall-clock time. We retain the PEIR symbolic formulation as a starting point and replace discrete counters by relaxed, parameterized soft counts. For each counter index ii we introduce an individual temperature τi\tau_{i} and define

f~i​(ω)=σ⁡(ci​(ω)−μiτi),\tilde{f}_{i}(\omega)\;=\;\sigma\!\Bigl(\frac{c_{i}(\omega)-\mu_{i}}{\tau_{i}}\Bigr), (2)

where σ\sigma denotes the logistic sigmoid, ci​(ω)c_{i}(\omega) is the measured or analytically estimated counter for configuration ω\omega, μi\mu_{i} is a centering constant, and τi>0\tau_{i}>0 is the branch-specific relaxation temperature. Here f~i​(ω)\tilde{f}_{i}(\omega) is the differentiable surrogate of the original integer counter fif_{i}.

We enforce monotonicity relative to an order over configurations. Let ω+\omega^{+} denote a configuration that is more aggressive (for example larger retrieval cutoff kk or smaller block-size) than ω\omega. We introduce a monotonicity conservation loss

Lmono=∑iReLU⁡(f~i​(ω+)−f~i​(ω)),L_{\mathrm{mono}}\;=\;\sum_{i}\operatorname{ReLU}\!\bigl(\tilde{f}_{i}(\omega^{+})-\tilde{f}_{i}(\omega)\bigr), (3)

where ReLU⁡(x)=max⁡(0,x)\operatorname{ReLU}(x)=\max(0,x). The loss penalizes violations of the expected monotone ordering; during training τi\tau_{i} are optimized subject to this loss alongside standard reconstruction/regression objectives.

To certify the learned relaxations we compute a monotonicity diagnostic per branch using the Pearson correlation between true integer counts and f~i\tilde{f}_{i} over an offline validation grid. We require

Pearson⁡(fitrue,f~i)> 0.98,\operatorname{Pearson}(\,f_{i}^{\text{true}},\;\tilde{f}_{i}\,)\;>\;0.98, (4)

where failure triggers either reinitialization of τi\tau_{i} or replacement of that branch by a conservative, non-differentiable estimator.

We additionally use a two-phase schedule for τi\tau_{i} during sampling: an exploration phase with larger τi\tau_{i} followed by a refinement phase with smaller τi\tau_{i}. Concretely,

τi​(t)={τi(0)if ​t<Texplore,τi(0)⋅ρ(t−Texplore)if ​t≥Texplore,\tau_{i}(t)\;=\;\begin{cases}\tau_{i}^{(0)}&\text{if }t<T_{\mathrm{explore}},\\[4.0pt] \tau_{i}^{(0)}\cdot\rho^{\,(t-T_{\mathrm{explore}})}&\text{if }t\geq T_{\mathrm{explore}},\end{cases} (5)

where tt is the Langevin step index, TexploreT_{\mathrm{explore}} marks the switch to refinement, ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) controls decay, and τi(0)\tau_{i}^{(0)} is an initialization possibly dependent on query characteristics (see Section 3.9). The schedule reduces bias caused by excessive smoothing while keeping gradients usable early in the trajectory.

3.4 Green potential formulation

To enable gradient-based optimization under efficiency and quality constraints, we introduce a differentiable green potential that maps a candidate configuration to a scalar energy value. Given a soft configuration ω^=D⁡(z)\hat{\omega}=D(z) decoded from a latent variable zz, the potential is defined as

U⁡(ω^)=α​Carbon​(ω^)+β​Latency​(ω^)+γ​Effectiveness​(ω^),U(\hat{\omega})=\alpha\,\mathrm{Carbon}(\hat{\omega})+\beta\,\mathrm{Latency}(\hat{\omega})+\gamma\,\mathrm{Effectiveness}(\hat{\omega}), (6)

where α,β,γ≥0\alpha,\beta,\gamma\geq 0 are weighting coefficients that regulate the relative importance of environmental cost, execution time, and retrieval quality, respectively.

The carbon and latency terms are obtained from the differentiable PEIR model, which provides relaxed operation counts as continuous surrogates. The carbon cost is expressed as

Carbon⁡(ω^)=kM​Mop​(ω^)+kF​Flop​(ω^),\mathrm{Carbon}(\hat{\omega})=k_{M}\,\mathrm{Mop}(\hat{\omega})+k_{F}\,\mathrm{Flop}(\hat{\omega}), (7)

where Mop⁡(ω^)\mathrm{Mop}(\hat{\omega}) and Flop⁡(ω^)\mathrm{Flop}(\hat{\omega}) denote the estimated memory and floating-point operation counts associated with ω^\hat{\omega}, and kMk_{M} and kFk_{F} are hardware-specific carbon intensity coefficients.

Similarly, the end-to-end latency is modeled as

Latency⁡(ω^)=TM​Mop​(ω^)+TF​Flop​(ω^),\mathrm{Latency}(\hat{\omega})=T_{M}\,\mathrm{Mop}(\hat{\omega})+T_{F}\,\mathrm{Flop}(\hat{\omega}), (8)

where TMT_{M} and TFT_{F} represent the amortized execution time per memory and floating-point operation, respectively. The effectiveness component serves as a lightweight quality regularizer and is approximated using a compact distilled evaluator applied to a small sampled document set:

Effectiveness​(ω^)=−Recall^​(ω^),\mathrm{Effectiveness}(\hat{\omega})=-\,\widehat{\mathrm{Recall}}(\hat{\omega}), (9)

where Recall^​(ω^)\widehat{\mathrm{Recall}}(\hat{\omega}) denotes a fast proxy for retrieval recall. The negative sign ensures that configurations with higher estimated effectiveness correspond to lower potential values.

All terms in U⁡(ω^)U(\hat{\omega}) are differentiable with respect to ω^\hat{\omega} and, by composition with the decoder DD, differentiable with respect to the latent variable zz. This property makes the proposed potential directly amenable to gradient-based sampling and underpins the retrieval-guided Langevin dynamics introduced in Equation (12).

3.5 Retrieval model: learning performance-consistent embeddings

To avoid learning spurious correlations between word-level semantics and configuration choices, we replace pure lexical contrastive objectives by a performance-consistency objective. Define a binary relation on query pairs: (q1,q2)(q_{1},q_{2}) is a performance-positive pair for configuration ω\omega if the observed recall difference satisfies |recallω​(q1)−recallω​(q2)|<δ|\text{recall}_{\omega}(q_{1})-\text{recall}_{\omega}(q_{2})|<\delta for a small threshold δ\delta (we use δ=1%\delta=1\% in practice). Positive query pairs thus share similar retrieval performance under ω\omega.

Let uq∈ℝ256u_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{256} be the query embedding produced by a compact encoder and vz∈ℝ256v_{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{256} the configuration embedding produced by an MLP. We define a hybrid similarity

V⁡(q,z)=uq⊤​vz+MLP⁡([uq;vz;uq⊙vz]),V(q,z)\;=\;u_{q}^{\top}v_{z}\;+\;\mathrm{MLP}\!\bigl([u_{q};\,v_{z};\,u_{q}\odot v_{z}]\bigr), (10)

where [⋅;⋅][\,\cdot\,;\,\cdot\,] denotes vector concatenation and ⊙\odot denotes elementwise product. The additional cross-tower MLP models fine-grained interactions that a pure dot product would miss.

Training uses a contrastive loss that treats performance-positive query pairs as positives and other pairs as negatives. Let ℬ\mathcal{B} denote a batch of queries with associated latent configurations. The loss per anchor query qq is a temperature-scaled NT-Xent variant conditioned on performance labels:

ℒperf=−∑q∈ℬlogexp⁡(V⁡(q,z+)/τc)∑z′∈ℬexp⁡(V⁡(q,z′)/τc),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{perf}}\;=\;-\sum_{q\in\mathcal{B}}\log\frac{\exp\bigl(V(q,z^{+})/\tau_{c}\bigr)}{\sum_{z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}}\exp\bigl(V(q,z^{\prime})/\tau_{c}\bigr)}, (11)

where z+z^{+} is any configuration whose performance on queries paired with qq meets the δ\delta criterion and τc\tau_{c} is the contrastive temperature. This objective biases the retrieval model to associate queries with configurations that yield empirically similar performance rather than with purely lexical neighbors.

At inference time we apply a safety rollback: if a decoded candidate ω^\hat{\omega} causes measured recall to drop more than a threshold ϵrecall\epsilon_{\mathrm{recall}} (e.g., 2%2\%) relative to the baseline, the sampler reverts to the previous latent zt−1z_{t-1} and halves the retrieval attraction coefficient γ2\gamma_{2} for subsequent steps. This mechanism prevents runaway drift toward low-quality yet low-carbon configurations.

3.6 Retrieval-guided Langevin with operational safeguards

Sampling proceeds in latent space with combined green potential and retrieval guidance. The discrete update is

zt+1=zt−γ1​∇zU​(D⁡(zt))+γ2​∇zV​(q,zt)+2​γ3​ξt,z_{t+1}=z_{t}-\gamma_{1}\nabla_{z}U\bigl(D(z_{t})\bigr)+\gamma_{2}\nabla_{z}V(q,z_{t})+\sqrt{2\gamma_{3}}\,\xi_{t}, (12)

where ξt∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\xi_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), γ1,γ2,γ3>0\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3}>0 are step coefficients, UU is defined in Equation (6), and DD denotes the decoder. To limit unnecessary iterations an early exit criterion is applied: if the relative decrease in potential over a sliding window of ww steps satisfies

U⁡(D⁡(zt−w))−U⁡(D⁡(zt))U⁡(D⁡(zt−w))<ϵU,\frac{U(D(z_{t-w}))-U(D(z_{t}))}{U(D(z_{t-w}))}<\epsilon_{U}, (13)

and t≥tmint\geq t_{\min}, then the loop terminates early. Typical choices are w=5w=5, ϵU=10−3\epsilon_{U}=10^{-3}, and tmin=6t_{\min}=6.

Each gradient evaluation for ∇zU​(D​(z))\nabla_{z}U(D(z)) traverses the decoder and Diff-PEIR graph. To reduce per-step cost we quantize PEIR MLP weights to 8-bit during inference and perform quantized backpropagation; empirical quantization noise is bounded and incorporated into the monotonicity test in Equation (4).

3.7 Validate, project and repair decoded configurations

The mapping from soft configuration ω^=D⁡(z)\hat{\omega}=D(z) to an integer, constraint-satisfying deployable configuration ω∗\omega^{\ast} is critical. We perform a two-stage constrained projection followed by repair. The projection solves a nearest-point problem with integer and modular constraints:

ωproj=arg⁡minω∈𝒞⁡∥ω−ω^∥2\omega^{\mathrm{proj}}=\arg\min_{\omega\in\mathcal{C}}\lVert\omega-\hat{\omega}\rVert_{2} (14)

where 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the feasible set (for example block-size must be a multiple of 64, k∈[1,104]k\in[1,10^{4}], quantization bits in {4,8}\{4,8\}). The projection is implemented using a lightweight integer solver (e.g., OR-Tools CP-SAT or an integer least squares heuristic) that respects linear modular constraints.

If the projected configuration induces a recall drop exceeding ϵproj\epsilon_{\mathrm{proj}} (e.g., 1%1\%) the repair phase performs a small local discrete search within 𝒞\mathcal{C}, exploring coordinate steps of magnitude one (or the smallest feasible step for modular constraints) until the recall is recovered or a budgeted number of steps is exhausted.

3.8 Online calibration: EW-RLS and PUE correction

To avoid unstable batch re-estimation we replace ordinary least squares with an online Exponentially Weighted Recursive Least Squares (EW-RLS) estimator for the latency and carbon mappings. Let θt\theta_{t} denote the coefficient vector at time tt (for latency θ\theta holds [TM,TF]⊤[T_{M},T_{F}]^{\top}) and xt=[Mop⁡(ωt),Flop⁡(ωt)]⊤x_{t}=[\mathrm{Mop}(\omega_{t}),\mathrm{Flop}(\omega_{t})]^{\top} the predictor. The EW-RLS updates are

Kt\displaystyle K_{t} =Pt−1​xt​(λ+xt⊤​Pt−1​xt)−1,\displaystyle=P_{t-1}x_{t}\bigl(\lambda+x_{t}^{\top}P_{t-1}x_{t}\bigr)^{-1}, (15)
θt\displaystyle\theta_{t} =θt−1+Kt​(yt−xt⊤​θt−1),\displaystyle=\theta_{t-1}+K_{t}\bigl(y_{t}-x_{t}^{\top}\theta_{t-1}\bigr), (16)
Pt\displaystyle P_{t} =1λ​(Pt−1−Kt​xt⊤​Pt−1),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\lambda}\bigl(P_{t-1}-K_{t}x_{t}^{\top}P_{t-1}\bigr), (17)

where yty_{t} is the measured latency (or carbon) for sample tt, PtP_{t} is the covariance matrix, KtK_{t} is the gain, and λ∈(0.95,0.99)\lambda\in(0.95,0.99) is the forgetting factor. These updates process each new measurement online and exponentially downweight older data. In Equations (15)–(17), matrix dimensions are consistent with the predictor size; the initial P0P_{0} is chosen large to reflect initial uncertainty.

Carbon coefficients are corrected for facility PUE variability. Let PUE⁡(t)\mathrm{PUE}(t) denote the instantaneous PUE read from the datacenter management interface. We apply a multiplicative correction

kM​(t)=kM(0)⋅PUE⁡(t)PUEref,k_{M}(t)=k_{M}^{(0)}\cdot\frac{\mathrm{PUE}(t)}{\mathrm{PUE}_{\mathrm{ref}}}, (18)

where kM(0)k_{M}^{(0)} is a baseline coefficient and PUEref\mathrm{PUE}_{\mathrm{ref}} is the reference PUE used during calibration.

To prevent oscillatory re-estimation the calibration procedure is triggered only when both a minimum buffer size is reached and the recent predictive performance degrades. Let MAErecent\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{recent}} be the moving mean absolute error over the last mm observations. Calibration is invoked only if

buffer_size>NminandMAErecent>ϵMAE,\text{buffer\_size}>N_{\min}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{recent}}>\epsilon_{\mathrm{MAE}}, (19)

with typical values Nmin=200N_{\min}=200 and ϵMAE=0.05\epsilon_{\mathrm{MAE}}=0.05 (i.e., 5%5\%).

3.9 Engineering budget: early exit, caching and quantized inference

To meet strict per-query latency budgets we use a combination of early stopping, frequency caching, and quantized inference. Early stopping uses the criterion in Equation (13). The system maintains a cache of precomputed optimal configurations for a small set of high-frequency query clusters obtained by clustering the training queries and storing the per-cluster best configuration. At runtime the pipeline first probes this cache; only on a cache miss does it invoke the RG-Langevin sampler.

Inference quantization reduces per-step gradient cost. PEIR internals and small MLPs are quantized to 8 bits; quantized backprop introduces bounded bias that is monitored by the monotonicity diagnostic (Equation (4)) and the online MAE metric in Equation (19).

4 Evaluation

This section evaluates GaiaFlow along three dimensions: the fidelity of the proposed latency models, the empirical relationship between predicted memory operations and measured latency, and the practical data collection requirements for coefficient estimation. All experiments aim to quantify model correctness and to demonstrate that GaiaFlow reduces operation counts and end-to-end latency under the same retrieval framework used in prior work.

4.1 Experimental setup

We use the MS-MARCO v1 development set[57], containing approximately 9.9M passages and 6,980 queries. Experiments focus on retrieval-time efficiency with preprocessed queries and a pre-built inverted index[58]. Query evaluation uses the Block-Max MaxScore (BMM) algorithm implemented in the PISA library[59]; BMM was selected for consistency with prior efficiency studies and for its competitive latency. The retrieval cutoff is set to k=1000k=1000. Except for classical BM25 baselines, quantized indexes are employed where applicable. Each reported measurement is the mean of five independent runs; latencies are reported in milliseconds and all timing experiments execute on a single logical core.

To validate portability, we collected instrumentation and timing data on two CPUs: an AMD EPYC 7402P and an Intel Xeon Gold 5118. Two PISA builds were produced: an instrumented build that records per-query operation counters for coefficient estimation, and a timed build with lightweight timers to measure wall-clock query latency. Instrumentation and timing were kept separate to avoid measurement interference.

Model goodness-of-fit is quantified using the coefficient of determination R2R^{2}:

R2= 1−∑i(yi−y^i)2∑i(yi−y¯)2,R^{2}\;=\;1-\frac{\sum_{i}(y_{i}-\hat{y}_{i})^{2}}{\sum_{i}(y_{i}-\bar{y})^{2}}, (20)

where yiy_{i} denotes the measured latency for query ii, y^i\hat{y}_{i} denotes the model prediction, and y¯\bar{y} is the sample mean of measured latencies. Values closer to one indicate a better fit.

4.2 Visualization

Figures 2–7 present a comprehensive visualization of the empirical behavior of GaiaFlow. The figures cover carbon prediction accuracy, latency and computational cost distributions, coefficient stability under subsampling, configuration-level Pareto trade-offs, online calibration dynamics, and representative Langevin optimization trajectories. All reported statistics are averaged over five independent random seeds where applicable, with shaded regions or distribution extents indicating one standard deviation. Together, these visualizations illustrate the efficiency–accuracy trade-offs and optimization characteristics of the proposed framework.

4.3 Model correctness

We first validate the latency models by fitting several variants and reporting R2R^{2} (Table 1). Variants include Mop-only (memory operations), Flop-only (floating-point operations), combined MFlop, a coefficient-only linear regression (LR) fitted on measured latencies, and a simple posting-list baseline (PL). Table 1 lists R2R^{2} for a set of retrieval methods on both Intel and AMD machines. Mop-based and combined models consistently achieve high R2R^{2} values for most methods, supporting the use of operation-based surrogates derived from the differentiable PEIR pipeline. Flop-only models perform poorly in our setup because query evaluation is predominantly memory-bound; combining memory and floating-point counts yields modest improvements. The LR variant attains very high R2R^{2} by leveraging measured latencies, but it is less interpretable than Mop-based models. Table 1 also includes GaiaFlow evaluated under the same protocol; GaiaFlow attains the highest or near-highest R2R^{2} across model variants, indicating that the differentiable PEIR combined with online calibration yields highly predictive operation-based latency estimates.

4.4 Correlation between Mop and latency

A desirable property of PEIR-style analysis is hardware-agnostic efficiency comparison. Table 2 reports mean latency on AMD and Intel platforms and mean Mop per method; ratios are shown relative to BM25. The relative ordering induced by Mop closely matches the ordering by measured latency for all methods, and the relative ratios are consistent across hardware platforms. These observations confirm that Mop serves as a robust, platform-independent indicator of relative retrieval efficiency. In our experiments GaiaFlow achieves lower average Mop and lower mean latency than several baselines, demonstrating that retrieval-guided latent sampling can find configurations that reduce operation counts while respecting retrieval quality constraints.

4.5 Ablation on Retrieval-Guided Attraction

To assess the specific contribution of the attraction component ∇zV​(q,z)\nabla_{z}V(q,z) within the retrieval-guided update, we construct a variant of the model, denoted GaiaFlowγ2=0{}_{\gamma_{2}=0}, by disabling the attraction coefficient while keeping all remaining hyperparameters unchanged. This setting allows us to isolate the effect of the semantic guidance on the sampler’s behavior. As reported in Table 3, removing the attraction term maintains the overall ranking quality, with recall essentially unaffected, yet it leads to a noticeable increase in computational cost. The sampler requires additional Langevin iterations before meeting the early-stopping condition, which results in higher latency and carbon expenditure. This observation suggests that the attraction signal facilitates faster convergence of the sampling trajectory rather than compensating with a quality–efficiency trade-off. A paired two-tailed t-test on the per-query latency of GaiaFlow versus GaiaFlowγ2=0{}_{\gamma_{2}=0} yields p=0.002p\!=\!0.002 (n=6980n\!=\!6980), confirming that the 0.9 ms reduction is statistically significant.

4.6 Data collection requirements

Estimating latency-model coefficients (for example, the latency coefficients TM,TFT_{M},T_{F} in Equation (8)) requires collecting per-query counters, which can be costly if performed exhaustively. We therefore evaluated sampling strategies to reduce instrumentation overhead. Randomly subsampling 5% of the queries yields coefficient estimates and fitted models that closely match those derived from the full set in our tests, with negligible loss in predictive accuracy. This indicates that practical coefficient estimation for online calibration can be achieved with modest instrumentation and limited sampling.

4.7 Parameter Sensitivity

To examine whether GaiaFlow depends on carefully tuned constants, we independently adjust each step coefficient γ1\gamma_{1}, γ2\gamma_{2}, and γ3\gamma_{3} while keeping the other two fixed. This single-factor analysis enables a clear view of how each parameter influences efficiency and retrieval quality. Table 4 reports the average latency, computational cost, recall, and carbon footprint across five repeated trials, together with the corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Perturbations of approximately ±10%\pm 10\% around the default setting lead to only minor variations in runtime and carbon usage, with changes remaining within 6% and 7% respectively. These results indicate that GaiaFlow behaves robustly under moderate deviations of its step-size parameters.

4.8 Cross-Platform Portability of Latency Coefficients

To assess whether the latency surrogate estimated on one processor can be applied to a different micro-architecture, we train the latency parameters [TM,TF][T_{\mathrm{M}},T_{\mathrm{F}}] on the AMD EPYC 7402P and evaluate the resulting model on an Intel Xeon Gold 5118 without additional fitting, and vice versa. This experiment directly tests the transferability of the differentiable PEIR latency formulation. Table 5 presents the coefficient of determination (R2R^{2}) and the mean absolute error between the predicted and measured latency on the target platform. In both transfer directions, the reduction in R2R^{2} is below 0.010.01 and the MAE remains under 0.450.45 ms, indicating that the learned latency model generalises well across distinct CPU architectures.

4.9 Summary

GaiaFlow achieves accurate latency prediction through differentiable PEIR with online calibration, delivers hardware-agnostic efficiency gains via Mop, consistently outperforms baselines in latency and Mop reduction, and requires only a small query sample for stable coefficient estimation.

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we introduced GaiaFlow, a transformative framework designed to pioneer ecological sustainability within the information retrieval domain through the application of semantic-guided diffusion tuning. This architecture specifically addresses the growing conflict between high-performance neural retrieval and its burgeoning computational power demand by establishing a resource-efficient optimization paradigm. By transcending the conventional reliance on hardware-specific latency measurements and focusing instead on fundamental operational overhead, our approach establishes a standardized and reliable foundation for carbon-frugal search operations. The strategic orchestration of retrieval-guided Langevin dynamics coupled with adaptive early exit protocols and quantized inference facilitates a substantial reduction in energy expenditure while simultaneously maintaining competitive retrieval effectiveness. Our empirical evaluations substantiate that utilizing hardware-agnostic performance modeling offers a scalable and effective roadmap for the engineering of environmentally conscious search infrastructures. Future research will focus on extending these carbon-aware optimization strategies to encompass dynamic and real-time multimodal retrieval environments.

𝒲2​(μt,π)≤(1−m​γ32)t​𝒲2​(μ0,π)+3​γ2​LV​Dm,\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu_{t},\pi)\leq\Bigl(1-\tfrac{m\gamma_{3}}{2}\Bigr)^{t}\mathcal{W}_{2}(\mu_{0},\pi)+\tfrac{3\gamma_{2}L_{V}D}{m}, (23)

where μt\mu_{t} is the law of ztz_{t} and π∝e−U/γ3\pi\propto e^{-U/\gamma_{3}}.

where 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} denotes the 2-Wasserstein distance, D⁡(z)D(z) is the decoder mapping, LL and mm are smoothness/strong-convexity constants of UU, LVL_{V} is the Lipschitz constant of ∇zV\nabla_{z}V, and DD is defined in (21). ‖zt+1−zt+1′‖≤‖zt−zt′−γ1​(∇U​(D⁡(zt))−∇U​(D⁡(zt′)))‖+γ2​LV​‖zt−zt′‖.\|z_{t+1}-z^{\prime}_{t+1}\|\leq\|z_{t}-z^{\prime}_{t}-\gamma_{1}(\nabla U(D(z_{t}))-\nabla U(D(z^{\prime}_{t})))\|+\gamma_{2}L_{V}\|z_{t}-z^{\prime}_{t}\|. (24)

A.2 Unbiasedness and Covariance of EW-RLS

Consider the linear model yt=xt⊤​θ∗+ηty_{t}=x_{t}^{\top}\theta^{\ast}+\eta_{t} with zero-mean independent noise ηt\eta_{t} having sub-Gaussian proxy σ2\sigma^{2}. The EW-RLS recursions are

Kt\displaystyle K_{t} =Pt−1​xt​(λ+xt⊤​Pt−1​xt)−1,\displaystyle=P_{t-1}x_{t}(\lambda+x_{t}^{\top}P_{t-1}x_{t})^{-1}, (26)
θt\displaystyle\theta_{t} =θt−1+Kt​(yt−xt⊤​θt−1),\displaystyle=\theta_{t-1}+K_{t}(y_{t}-x_{t}^{\top}\theta_{t-1}), (27)
Pt\displaystyle P_{t} =λ−1​(Pt−1−Kt​xt⊤​Pt−1).\displaystyle=\lambda^{-1}(P_{t-1}-K_{t}x_{t}^{\top}P_{t-1}). (28)

where λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) is the forgetting factor.

Proposition A.2.

If 𝔼⁡[θ0]=θ∗\mathbb{E}[\theta_{0}]=\theta^{\ast} then for all tt the estimator is unbiased: 𝔼⁡[θt]=θ∗\mathbb{E}[\theta_{t}]=\theta^{\ast}. Moreover

𝔼​‖θt−θ∗‖2=σ2​tr​(Pt),\mathbb{E}\|\theta_{t}-\theta^{\ast}\|^{2}=\sigma^{2}\mathrm{tr}(P_{t}), (29)

and under ‖xt‖2≤Bx\|x_{t}\|^{2}\leq B_{x} and tr⁡(P0)≤T0\mathrm{tr}(P_{0})\leq T_{0} we have

𝔼​‖θt−θ∗‖2≤σ2​(λt​T0+d​Bx1−λ).\mathbb{E}\|\theta_{t}-\theta^{\ast}\|^{2}\leq\sigma^{2}\Bigl(\lambda^{t}T_{0}+\frac{dB_{x}}{1-\lambda}\Bigr). (30)

where tr⁡(⋅)\mathrm{tr}(\cdot) is the matrix trace, dd is parameter dimension, BxB_{x} bounds regressor norm, and T0T_{0} bounds tr⁡(P0)\mathrm{tr}(P_{0}). Taking expectation in (27) and using 𝔼⁡[ηt]=0\mathbb{E}[\eta_{t}]=0 yields 𝔼⁡[θt]=𝔼⁡[θt−1]\mathbb{E}[\theta_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[\theta_{t-1}] when 𝔼⁡[θt−1]=θ∗\mathbb{E}[\theta_{t-1}]=\theta^{\ast}, hence unbiasedness by induction. Define et=θt−θ∗e_{t}=\theta_{t}-\theta^{\ast}; standard RLS algebra gives 𝔼⁡[et​et⊤]=σ2​Pt\mathbb{E}[e_{t}e_{t}^{\top}]=\sigma^{2}P_{t}, so (29) holds. From (28) one can show the scalar recursion tr⁡(Pt)≤λ​tr​(Pt−1)+d​Bx\mathrm{tr}(P_{t})\leq\lambda\,\mathrm{tr}(P_{t-1})+dB_{x}; iterating yields the bound in (30). ∎

A.3 Quantization Error Bound

Let gUg_{U} be the exact gradient and g~U\tilde{g}_{U} its uniform 8-bit quantization with step Δ\Delta. Uniform rounding implies

‖g~U−gU‖∞≤Δ2,\|\tilde{g}_{U}-g_{U}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{\Delta}{2}, (31)

where ∥⋅∥∞\|\cdot\|_{\infty} is the maximum absolute coordinate error. Assuming the carbon surrogate C^\widehat{C} is Lipschitz in the gradient with sensitivity coefficients kM,kFk_{M},k_{F} applied to operation-count vectors Mop,Flop\mathrm{Mop},\mathrm{Flop}, a first-order bound gives

|C^quant−C^|≤Δ2​(kM​‖Mop‖1+kF​‖Flop‖1),\bigl|\widehat{C}_{\mathrm{quant}}-\widehat{C}\bigr|\leq\frac{\Delta}{2}\bigl(k_{M}\|\mathrm{Mop}\|_{1}+k_{F}\|\mathrm{Flop}\|_{1}\bigr), (32)

where ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1} is the vector 1-norm. For Δ≤8×10−4\Delta\leq 8\times 10^{-4} this evaluates below 0.050.05 g CO2 in our workloads. For recall, let s(K)s_{(K)} and s(K+1)s_{(K+1)} be the KK-th and (K+1)(K+1)-th exact scores; define Δmargin=s(K)−s(K+1)\Delta_{\mathrm{margin}}=s_{(K)}-s_{(K+1)}. If per-item score perturbation obeys maxi⁡|s~i−si|≤δ<Δmargin/2\max_{i}|\tilde{s}_{i}-s_{i}|\leq\delta<\Delta_{\mathrm{margin}}/2 then top-KK is unchanged. Combining a model-dependent constant CsC_{s} with (31) gives maxi⁡|s~i−si|≤Cs​Δ/2\max_{i}|\tilde{s}_{i}-s_{i}|\leq C_{s}\Delta/2; thus if Cs​Δ/2<Δmargin/2C_{s}\Delta/2<\Delta_{\mathrm{margin}}/2 recall is preserved. Empirically for our tasks Δ≤8×10−4\Delta\leq 8\times 10^{-4} yields recall drop within 0.3%0.3\%. ∎
